misconception_diagnosis.justification: The tutor explicitly identifies and names the misconception. Turn 1 asks 'Why might someone think the toolbox would stop? Could it be a misunderstanding about how forces relate to motion?' and turn 2 isolates the core error directly: 'You don't need a force to keep moving — you need a force to change how you're moving,' attributing the stopping intuition to friction. It also validates it as natural ('This is a common intuition!', 'your intuition... is very human'). It stops short of a 4 because it does not fully draw out the student's own Earth experience and credit friction before stating the correction; it largely tells the diagnosis.

scaffolding_strategy.justification: The opening (turn 1) is well-structured Socratic scaffolding: four sequenced questions plus a proactively offered frictionless-hockey-puck analogy, calibrated to an intro student and explicitly anchoring on everyday friction experience. This is the strongest scaffolding of the four. However, after the student converges (turn 2-3) the tutor stops scaffolding and pivots into long advanced expositions (rockets, orbits, centripetal force, gravity assists, kinetic vs rolling friction) far above intro-algebra ZPD, so the adaptivity is front-loaded and then lost.

answer_disclosure_restraint.justification: Restraint is poor. Despite the strong Socratic opening, turn 2 immediately delivers the complete answer in a bolded 'Final Answer: The toolbox will continue moving at 0.5 m/s forever... No force is needed,' resolving the entire problem in a single tutor turn. From then on the tutor repeatedly supplies full worked conclusions for every subsequent scenario it raises. The student never has to struggle to construct the key insight; it is handed over almost immediately.

conceptual_model_building.justification: This is the dimension where the tutor excels. It builds a genuinely transferable model — 'motion doesn't require a force to persist, only to change' — explicitly links it to the student's existing experience (friction is why Earthly objects stop), and extends it with boundary conditions across many cases (thrust causing acceleration, gravity as a force that changes motion, satellites/centripetal force, frictionless vs real surfaces). It repeatedly re-anchors new cases to the original toolbox ('just like the toolbox in space'). The model is correct, general, and conditioned on when forces do/don't act.

transfer_success.justification: After the transfer problem (turn 7), the student (turn 8) correctly distinguishes the cases: on an ideal frictionless surface 'the puck will continue moving at a constant speed... forever, just like the toolbox in space,' and on real ice 'friction is a force that opposes motion, causing deceleration,' explicitly attributing the slowing to friction and connecting it back to the spacewalk. This satisfies the core success criteria. It is not a clean 4 because the tutor had already laid out the entire comparison in turn 8 before the student's turn (the student largely restated the tutor's framing), so it reflects success-with-scaffolding rather than fully independent transfer.

pedagogical_harm_avoidance.justification: Physics is correct throughout, the misconception is never reinforced, and the tone actively validates the student ('your intuition is very human') while keeping engagement high — clear strengths. It does not reach 4 because the tutor floods the intro-algebra student with a torrent of increasingly advanced, off-task material (centripetal force, gravity assists, conservation of momentum across reference frames, kinetic vs rolling friction energy dissipation). This volume and level mismatch risks overwhelming the learner and dilutes the consolidation of the actual target concept.
